nameStory: The woodland vole gets its name from its preference for forested areas, unlike its meadow-dwelling cousins who stick to open grasslands. It's also called the pine vole because it's often found in pine forests, though it's not picky about which type of trees it lives under. The name 'vole' comes from the Norwegian word 'voll,' meaning field, even though this particular species prefers the woods!
description: The woodland vole is a tiny, chunky rodent about the size of your thumb, with a rounded body and stubby tail. These little furballs have small eyes, nearly hidden ears, and soft, dense fur that's typically brownish-gray on top and lighter underneath. They're built like tiny bulldozers, perfectly designed for their underground lifestyle. Adults typically measure 3-4 inches long with a tail that's only about an inch long.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Compact and cylindrical, about the size of a large grape with a stubby tail shorter than its body - feels dense and solid if handled, like a small furry sausage

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Incredibly soft, dense fur that feels almost velvety to the touch - rusty brown to grayish-brown above with a lighter gray belly, much softer than other small rodents

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Tiny four-toed front prints and five-toed back prints, but tracks are rarely seen since they spend most time in underground tunnels

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Almost never seen above ground during daylight - active year-round but stays in tunnel systems, making soft scratching sounds in leaf litter

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Small round holes in the ground about the width of a quarter, often near tree roots, with tiny dark pellets nearby that smell faintly earthy

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always in wooded areas with loose, well-drained soil - look for their sign around deciduous trees and especially in areas with thick leaf litter

habitat: Woodland voles prefer deciduous and mixed forests with loose, well-drained soils that are easy to tunnel through. You'll find them in areas with thick leaf litter under oak, maple, and hickory trees, often on gentle slopes or well-drained bottomlands. They avoid wet, compacted soils and are rarely found in pure coniferous forests despite their 'pine vole' nickname.

seasonality.spring: Most active period for breeding, with soft squeaking sounds sometimes audible from tunnel entrances. Fresh dirt mounds and new holes appear around tree bases.
seasonality.summer: Continue underground activity but may venture briefly to surface during cool dawn hours. Look for chewed bark at ground level on young trees.
seasonality.fall: Busy collecting and storing nuts and seeds in underground chambers. Tunnel systems expand as they prepare winter food caches.
seasonality.winter: Remain active in tunnels under snow, creating elaborate runway systems. Their holes stay open even in light snow cover.

funFact: Woodland voles are such dedicated underground dwellers that they can live their entire lives without ever seeing sunlight - some individuals spend 99% of their time in tunnels, making them one of New England's most secretive mammals!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with shrews, but woodland voles have visible eyes and ears (shrews have tiny pin-dot eyes) and chunkier bodies. Remember: if it looks like a tiny, plump hamster with a stubby tail, it's probably a woodland vole. If it's skinny with a pointy nose like a tiny anteater, it's likely a shrew.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'pine voles,' they actually prefer hardwood forests over pine forests, making this common name quite misleading. The scientific name 'pinetorum' means 'of the pines,' but early naturalists apparently misidentified their preferred habitat.
compareHints: Woodland voles are much more secretive than Eastern meadow voles, which are commonly seen scurrying through grass in daylight. While meadow voles have longer tails (about half their body length) and prefer open areas, woodland voles have stubby tails and stick to forested areas. Woodland voles also have softer, denser fur and smaller ears than their meadow-dwelling relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Eastern Meadow Vole is larger and prefers more open, grassy areas compared to its cousin the Woodland Vole, which is smaller and sticks to forested areas with loose soil for burrowing underground.
